extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, dramatists, and students of poetics / dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama (structure, character, diction, song, spectacle, and specific plot devices such as reversal and recognition) according to classical poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of actions (not of men)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of Actions, not of Men; the poet imitates action (a sequence of events) rather than merely depicting characters or single incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority: design the action (fabula) as the primary object of imitation. Decoration and other parts (character, diction, song, spectacle) serve the imitation of action. Evaluate whether the play represents a coherent action rather than disconnected portrayals of persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six parts of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessary parts of tragedy are six: Fabula (Plot), Mores (Character), Dictio (Diction), Sententiae (Thought/Propositions), Apparatus (Spectacle/Stagecraft), & Modulation/Concentus (Song/Music).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot is the chief (the end); character comes second, then thought, diction, song, and spectacle. When assessing or composing, ensure each part is present and subordinate to the plot's imitation of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and wholeness of plot (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragic plot ought to be a whole with magnitude: it must have a beginning, a middle, and an end, i.e., a principium, a medium, & a finis, so that events follow with necessity or probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pick arbitrary starting or ending points—choose them so that the sequence is intelligible and the whole can be grasped and remembered. Check that removal or transposition of a part disrupts the whole (sign of unity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate magnitude (length)
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitation must have an apt magnitude: not so small that perception is confused, nor so large that attention is distracted — it should be large enough to be memorable and apprehendable in one view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a span of action that memory can easily retain; avoid overly protracted sequences (which break perception) or overly brief ones (which lack impact). The right magnitude supports the unity and emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single integrated action (avoid episodic multiplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: When imitation is of an action, the imitation ought to be of one entire action; the parts must be so disposed that removing or transposing any part destroys the whole. Episodic compositions (many disconnected actions) are defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer one central, integrated plotline over aggregating many unrelated episodes. Beware of adding episodes that do not arise naturally from the plot; such episodic fables are typical of poor poets or those relying on actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and necessity in sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in the plot should follow from one another either necessarily or probably; the poet composes what can be (probabiliter) or must be (necessario) rather than merely what has happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge transitions for plausibility: each event should be motivated by prior events in a way that is probable or necessary. Avoid improbable, gratuitous incidents that break causal or probable linkage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of plot over diction/character
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot (fabula) is the principle and almost the soul of tragedy; diction and character occupy lower positions. Poets should compose the plot first, then supply diction and characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a piece, treat excellence of plot as the principal criterion. Beware of works that emphasize fine phrasing or singular character sketches while neglecting coherent action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia is a change into the contrary of what had been (a reversal) — a turning of the action to the opposite, occurring by necessity or probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversal as a plot device to produce surprise and emotional effect; assess whether the reversal arises naturally from the preceding action and whether it contributes to unity and emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (agnitio / anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agnitio is a change from ignorance to knowledge about persons or circumstances; it may be produced by signs, natural tokens, letters, memory, syllogism, or contrivances of the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition is most effective when it arises from the facts themselves (probable and admiring) rather than obvious contrivances. Evaluate whether recognitions are credible and lead to pity and fear when coupled with reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of reversal and recognition (complex plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest (most pleasing) tragedies use both peripeteia and agnitio together — a complex plot that yields strong emotional effect (pity and fear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor plots where reversal and recognition are linked causally and arise from the plot's constitution. Avoid artificial insertions of these devices that do not proceed from prior events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos / Perturbation (suffering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of tragedy is the representation of extreme suffering and disasters (deaths before our eyes, grievous pains and wounds) — perturbation or pathos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include scenes of genuine suffering when they arise from the action; ensure they contribute to the whole and to the intended emotional response rather than serving mere spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character qualities for protagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters depicted should satisfy four conditions: (1) be good (boni), (2) be fitting/appropriate (convenientes) to their role, (3) be similar (similes) where similarity is required, and (4) be proportionately unequal/equal as the imitation demands (æquales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose characters whose moral and social attributes suit the actions they must perform. Avoid wholly vile or wholly perfect heroes; best are those of some standing who fall through a grave error or mischance (eliciting pity and fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate moral status of tragic hero (middle character)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist should not be perfectly virtuous nor thoroughly wicked; rather someone of esteem who falls through a serious error or offense (not through vice) — this produces pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid heroes whose fall comes from vice (which appears criminal rather than tragic) or heroes who are undeserving sufferers; prefer errors or misjudgments in otherwise admirable figures (e.g., Oedipus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid transitions from virtue to vice or vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should not show good people ruined by wickedness nor the wicked rising to felicity; such shifts are more appropriate to other genres and do not evoke proper tragic emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the reversal is caused by error or misfortune rather than moral corruption or reward for wickedness; the ethical orientation of outcome matters for the tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodic plot as anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: An episodic (episodicam) plot—where episodes follow one another without necessary or probable connection—is characteristic of inferior poets and of plays extended beyond their natural capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and avoid episodes that do not follow from the plot's internal logic. Episodic structure often stems from reliance on actors or spectacle rather than coherent composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus integration and function
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as part of the whole drama and ought to promote the action; in some usages the Chorus is treated as one of the characters and as part of the total structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether choric parts (parodos, stasimon, exodus) are integrated into and advance the plot rather than interrupting it; the Chorus should enhance, not replace, dramatic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of the dramatic structure (names & roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragedy's parts (in quantity and division) include Prologue, Episodium (episodes), Exodus, Choricum (and its parts Parodus and Stasimon); these are integral parts with specified placement: Prologus before chorus enters, Episodia between choric songs, Exodus after last chorus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or judging structure, verify that the play respects these functional divisions and that each serves its role in advancing unity and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of spectacle/apparatus subordinate to plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (apparatus) can move the audience but is less the poet's art and more the work of stagecraft; pity and fear must primarily arise from the action, not from mere visual effects or monstrous stagecraft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on scenic display alone to evoke tragic emotions. Evaluate whether spectacle supports the plot's causes and emotional logic rather than substituting for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language, diction, and rhetorical devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction (dictio) is the apt elocution of names and words; Sententiae (thought) are the propositions and faculty of saying what is natural and fitting (demonstrate, refute, move emotions, amplify/diminish). Figures of diction (metaphor, etc.) belong to proper poetic craftsmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge diction for fitness and clarity, rhetorical power, and appropriateness to characters and action. Figures (metaphors, ornament) should be used to illuminate character and action, not to obscure them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor and ornamental language as craft elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor is the transference of a name by genus/species/analogy and other figures of speech are part of diction; poets should polish language and choose proper words, metaphors, and ornaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate stylistic devices for their appropriateness and contribution to characterization and effect. Poor or intrusive ornament (e.g., irrelevant cleverness) harms dramatic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of recognition (types and ranking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions arise by (1) natural signs (e.g., scars), (2) external contrivances or poet's devices (letters, tokens), (3) memory (sudden remembrance), (4) syllogistic inference, or (5) false reasoning; the best recognitions are those springing from the facts themselves and exciting admiration by probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer recognitions that are plausible and intrinsic to the situation; judge contrived or artless recognitions as inferior. Recognitions that produce admiration and follow probabilistically from prior events are superior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation order: show the whole then episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should present the whole (the universe of the plot) first, then insert episodes; the universal should be evident before episodic insertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing, outline the entire sequence of actions (the whole) and ensure episodes are introduced only to serve that whole; avoid fragmentary presentation that obscures the unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solution (resolution) and connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Connection (connexion) consists of what is external and some internal elements; Solution (solutio) stretches from the point where the cause is alleged to the end — the resolution must derive from the established connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the denouement follows from established causes and connections in the plot; a resolution that lacks causal connection undermines the work's integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of tragic types
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds/species of tragedy: (1) Complex (with peripeteia & recognition), (2) Pathetic (pathē-based), (3) Ethical (ethic), and (4) Those depicting marvels or underworld matters — each demands different emphases but all should strive for unity and fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing genre specifics, ensure the play fulfills the demands of its species (e.g., emotive force for pathetic tragedies, moral inquiry for ethical tragedies) while maintaining unity and proper plotting.
